query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: CoCrFeMnNi-based high-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers can be used to probe and control the transition between diffusion-dominated and dislocation-mediated creep by tuning interface coherency through layer thickness and composition adjustments.
generation.material_initial_state: Fully dense, single-phase CoCrFeMnNi-based HEA multilayers, carefully deposited with uniform interface structures and minimal defect density.
generation.intervention: Vary the HEA layer thicknesses (e.g., from a few nanometers up to hundreds of nanometers) and locally adjust composition at interfaces to manipulate coherent vs. semi-coherent boundaries, then subject these multilayers to elevated temperatures to induce creep deformation.
generation.conditions: Moderate-to-high temperatures (approximately 400–700 °C) under controlled stresses representative of service creep conditions, combined with in-situ or ex-situ mechanical testing and high-resolution microstructural characterization.
generation.structural_mediator: Misfit dislocation networks forming at the HEA layer interfaces under higher interface mismatch, which alter the dominant creep mechanism as temperatures/stresses increase.
generation.mechanism: When interfaces remain highly coherent, creep is predominantly limited by diffusional processes across interface boundaries; as misfit strain accumulates and partial coherency is lost, dislocation-mediated mechanisms increasingly govern the creep response.
generation.predicted_outcome: A threshold interface mismatch or layer thickness will delineate the switch from slower, diffusion-controlled creep to faster, dislocation-driven creep, observable as a measurable change in creep strain rate.
generation.baseline: Highly coherent CoCrFeMnNi-based HEA multilayers showing diffusion-dominated creep at moderate service temperatures.
generation.boundary: The transition may shift if significant second-phase precipitation or large-scale defects develop, or if temperature/stresses exceed the operational ranges (above ~700 °C).
generation.uncertainty: Exact layer thicknesses and compositions for the transition are uncertain and may be sensitive to deposition conditions and minor alloying elements.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize multiple CoCrFeMnNi-based HEA multilayer sets with incrementally varied layer thickness (5–200 nm) and composition gradients to adjust interface coherency. Subject these samples to in-situ nanoindentation or micropillar creep tests at temperatures from 400 to 700 °C and measure creep rates. Characterize interfacial misfit and dislocation structures via high-resolution electron microscopy before and after testing. Compare the onset of dislocation-mediated creep with measured interface mismatch.
measurements: Creep strain rate under controlled loading conditions
Interface coherency and misfit dislocation density (using high-resolution microscopy)
Grain boundary and interface chemistry (using EDS or atom probe tomography)
Time to strain or failure under constant load
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Failure to detect a systematic correlation between increasing interface mismatch (or layer thickness) and a shift from diffusion-limited to dislocation-dominated creep would invalidate the hypothesis that CoCrFeMnNi-based HEA multilayers can be used to induce and observe this mechanism transition by tuning interface coherency.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

Abstract The microstructure, temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) were investigated. SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
